Content:
Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion [MATH: p] of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate [MATH: A.]"

Content:
If the company has [MATH: N = 50] employees, and [MATH: 30] of them will vote for candidate [MATH: A,] then the proportion [MATH: p] is given by

Content:
[MATH: p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6.]

Content:
In other words, [MATH: 60\%] of the company's employees will vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: N] is the population size
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion
- The number of employees that will vote for candidate [MATH: A] is given by
[MATH: Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30.]

Content:
In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating [MATH: p] in cases where the population size [MATH: N] is very large. Note that although the population size [MATH: N] is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas.

Content:
We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable [MATH: X_i,] defined by

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the population will vote for candidateA; 0, otherwise]
for [MATH: i = 1,\ldots,50.]

Content:
Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate [MATH: A] is straightforward:

Content:
[MATH: P(X_{i} = 1)|= (the number of members that will vote for candidateA)/(population size); = (Np)/(N); = (30)/(50); = 0.6]

Content:
Watch out! It's important to note that the [MATH: X_i]'s are dependent! For example,

Content:
[MATH: P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ).]

Content:
To see why, note that [MATH: P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,] as before. However,

Content:
[MATH: P(X_{2} = 1|X_{1} = 1)|= ((the number of members that will vote for candidateA) − 1)/(population size − 1); = (Np − 1)/(N − 1); = (50 ⋅ 0.6 − 1)/(50 − 1); = (30 − 1)/(49); = (29)/(49); ≈ 0.592; ≠ P(X_{2} = 1).]

Content:
Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate [MATH: A.] So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will also vote for candidate [MATH: A,] we consider a reduced population with [MATH: N-1 = 49] members, of which only [MATH: 30-1 = 29] will vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

sections.normalized_html:
We have a population of size [MATH: N = 50,] and [MATH: p = 0.6] represents the proportion of the population that will vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Therefore:

  • The number of members that will vote for candidate [MATH: A] equals [MATH: Np = 50(0.6) = 30.]

  • The number of members that will not vote for candidate [MATH: A] equals [MATH: N(1 - p) = 50(1 - 0.6) = 20.]

We select two members of the population at random. We need to find [MATH: P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0),] the probability that the second member will not vote for candidate [MATH: A] given that the first member will not vote for candidate [MATH: A] either.

If the first member does not vote for candidate [MATH: A,] we have

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: N - 1 = 50 - 1 = 49] members remaining, and

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: N(1 - p)-1 = 19] members remaining that will not vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Therefore, [MATH: P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0) = \dfrac{N(1 - p)-1}{N-1} = \dfrac{19}{49}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that a company is about to elect a new union representative. We're interested in determining the proportion [MATH: p] of a company's employees that will vote for "candidate [MATH: A.]"

Content:
If the company has [MATH: N = 50] employees, and [MATH: 30] of them will vote for candidate [MATH: A,] then the proportion [MATH: p] is given by

Content:
[MATH: p = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.6.]

Content:
In other words, [MATH: 60\%] of the company's employees will vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: N] is the population size
- [MATH: p] is the population proportion
- The number of employees that will vote for candidate [MATH: A] is given by
[MATH: Np = 50\cdot 0.6 = 30.]

Content:
In this lesson, our goal is to build foundations for estimating [MATH: p] in cases where the population size [MATH: N] is very large. Note that although the population size [MATH: N] is not very large in this example, we can still use it to help develop the key ideas.

Content:
We start by modeling the response from each member of the population as a random variable [MATH: X_i,] defined by

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the population will vote for candidateA; 0, otherwise]
for [MATH: i = 1,\ldots,50.]

Content:
Calculating the probability that a randomly selected member of the population will vote for candidate [MATH: A] is straightforward:

Content:
[MATH: P(X_{i} = 1)|= (the number of members that will vote for candidateA)/(population size); = (Np)/(N); = (30)/(50); = 0.6]

Content:
Watch out! It's important to note that the [MATH: X_i]'s are dependent! For example,

Content:
[MATH: P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \neq P(X_2 = 1 ).]

Content:
To see why, note that [MATH: P(X_2 = 1) = 0.6,] as before. However,

Content:
[MATH: P(X_{2} = 1|X_{1} = 1)|= ((the number of members that will vote for candidateA) − 1)/(population size − 1); = (Np − 1)/(N − 1); = (50 ⋅ 0.6 − 1)/(50 − 1); = (30 − 1)/(49); = (29)/(49); ≈ 0.592; ≠ P(X_{2} = 1).]

Content:
Let's interpret this result. We know that the first member will vote for candidate [MATH: A.] So, to compute the conditional probability that the second member will also vote for candidate [MATH: A,] we consider a reduced population with [MATH: N-1 = 49] members, of which only [MATH: 30-1 = 29] will vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Content:
Calculating [MATH: P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 0)] works similarly, as we'll see in the following example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Conditional Probability Given a Population Proportion

Example Prompt:
Workers of a small company decided to elect a new union representative. There are [MATH: 50] workers, and [MATH: 60\%] of this worker population will vote for candidate [MATH: A.] Let the random variable [MATH: X_i] be equal to
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the population will vote for candidateA; 0, otherwise]
for [MATH: i = 1,\ldots,50.] Find [MATH: P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We have a population of size [MATH: N = 50,] and [MATH: p = 0.6] represents the proportion of the population that will vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Therefore:

- The number of members that will vote for candidate [MATH: A] equals
[MATH: Np = 50(0.6) = 30.]
- The number of members that will not vote for candidate [MATH: A] equals
[MATH: N(1 - p) = 50(1 - 0.6) = 20.]

We select two members of the population at random. We need to find [MATH: P(X_2 = 0 | X_1
= 0),] the probability that the second member will not vote for candidate [MATH: A] given that the first member will not vote for candidate [MATH: A] either.

If the first member does not vote for candidate [MATH: A,] we have

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: N - 1 = 50 - 1 = 49] members remaining, and

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: N(1 - p)-1 = 19] members remaining that will not vote for candidate [MATH: A.]

Therefore,
[MATH: P(X_2 = 0 | X_1 = 0) = \dfrac{N(1 - p)-1}{N-1} = \dfrac{19}{49}.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Independence in Large Populations

Content:
Suppose we have a population of size [MATH: N=1\,000] of which the proportion [MATH: p=0.5] has a particular characteristic. We denote the random variable [MATH: X_i] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the population has the characteristic; 0, otherwise]
for [MATH: i = 1,\ldots,1\,000.]

Content:
Technically speaking, as we saw previously, the [MATH: X_i]'s are dependent.

Content:
This time, however, since the population size [MATH: N = 1\,000] is large, we may approximate that the [MATH: X_i]'s are independent.

Content:
To see why, we first note that

Content:
[MATH: P(X_2=1) = \dfrac{Np}{N} = 0.5.]

Content:
Now, computing [MATH: P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1),] we have

Content:
[MATH: P(X_{2} = 1|X_{1} = 1)|= (Np − 1)/(N − 1); = (1000 ⋅ 0.5 − 1)/(1000 − 1); = (500 − 1)/(999); = (499)/(999); ≈ 0.5.]

Content:
To summarize, we've shown that

Content:
[MATH: P(X_2 = 1 | X_1 = 1) \approx P(X_2 = 1),]

Content:
suggesting that [MATH: X_1] and [MATH: X_2] are (approximately) independent.

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Number of Sample Elements With a Characteristic

Content:
Now, suppose we conduct a random sample of size [MATH: n] where some proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable [MATH: X_i] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise]
for [MATH: i = 1,\ldots,n.]

Content:
It can be shown that the [MATH: X_i]'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables provided that the population size [MATH: N] is significantly larger than the sample size [MATH: n] (which we denote as [MATH: N \gg n]). In practice, this typically means that the sample size should be no larger than [MATH: 5\%] of the population size.

Content:
The assumption that the population size is much larger than the sample size is true in many cases. For example, the U.S. voting population consists of hundreds of millions of people, yet a typical sample from this population might consist of only a few thousand voters.

Content:
Let's now consider the following statistic:

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i]

Content:
where [MATH: X_i \sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).]

Content:
Since the [MATH: X_i]'s take the value [MATH: 1] if the [MATH: i]th element has the characteristic or [MATH: 0] if the [MATH: i]th element doesn't have the characteristic, the statistic [MATH: X] can be used to count the number of elements with the characteristic. In other words, [MATH: X] represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic.

Content:
We wish to determine the sampling distribution of [MATH: X.] Note the following:

Content:
- Each [MATH: X_i] can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, i.e., [MATH: X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p).]
- Since we're assuming that [MATH: N\gg n,] it follows that [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n] are (approximately) independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) Bernoulli random variables.
- It can be shown that a sum of [MATH: n] I.I.D. Bernoulli random variables with parameter [MATH: p] is a binomial random variable [MATH: B(n,p)] (we'll prove this in a separate lesson). Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).]

Content:
We summarize this process using the following flow chart.

Graphic:

Content:
Finally, using the formulas for the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable, we have the following approximations:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)]

[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise]

Now, provided that [MATH: N \gg n,] the random variables [MATH: X_i] can be considered independent and identically distributed. Under this assumption, we have
[MATH: X_i\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p) \qquad 1\leq i\leq n]
where [MATH: p] is the proportion of the population that has the characteristic.

Therefore, the random variable [MATH: X,] defined as
[MATH: X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i]
can be approximated as a binomial random variable [MATH: X\approx B(n,p),] where
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).]

In our case, we're told that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size. Moreover, we have
[MATH: p = 35 \% = 0.35, \qquad n = 360.]

Therefore,
[MATH: X\approx B(360,0.35)]
and we have the following results for the mean and variance:
[MATH: E[X]|= np; = 360 ⋅ 0.35; = 126; Var[X]|= np(1 − p); = 360 ⋅ 0.35 ⋅ (1 − 0.35); = 81.9]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Mean and Variance of Sample Proportions

Content:
Suppose we conduct a random sample of size [MATH: n] where some proportion [MATH: p] of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable [MATH: X_i] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: {1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise]
for [MATH: i = 1,\ldots,n.]

Content:
We know that if the population sample size [MATH: n] is small compared to the population size [MATH: N,] then the [MATH: X_i]'s can be modeled as mutually independent random variables. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: X = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i \approx B(n,p).]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: X] represents the number of sample elements with the characteristic. Therefore, we can form an estimate for the population proportion [MATH: p] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,p} = \dfrac{X}{n} = \dfrac1 n \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} X_i = \overline{X}]

Content:
Let's calculate the mean and variance of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.] First, recall that

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[X] = np, \qquad \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p).]

Content:
Therefore, for the mean of [MATH: \widehat{\,p},] we have

Content:
[MATH: E[p^(^)]|= E[(X)/(n)]; = (1)/(n) ⋅ E[X]; = (1)/(n) ⋅ np; = p.]

Content:
For the variance of [MATH: \widehat{\,p},] we have

Content:
[MATH: Var[p^(^)]|= Var[(X)/(n)]; = (1)/(n^{2}) ⋅ Var[X]; = (1)/(n^{2}) ⋅ np(1 − p); = (p(1 − p))/(n).]

Content:
To summarize, we have the following important results:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{E}[\widehat{\,p}] = p, \qquad \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}] = \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}]

Content:
It should be noted that we don't yet know the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}.] What we do know is that whatever the sampling distribution of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is, it has mean [MATH: p] and variance [MATH: \dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}.]

---

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Standard Error

Content:
The standard deviation of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] is called the standard error of [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] and is denoted [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}]\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}]} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}}]

Content:
If [MATH: p] is unknown, we can replace it with its estimate [MATH: \widehat{\,p}] in the standard error formula, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}] = \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}(1-\widehat{\,p})}{n}}]

Content:
Note that we have written [MATH: \widehat{\textrm{SE}}[\widehat{\,p}]] to denote that the above expression is an estimate of [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,p}] .]
